💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
  • It has been revealed that over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
  • Some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

It has been revealed that over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the newly introduced plants a little boost.

According to recent reports, nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

Recent findings suggest that nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Sources indicate that grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

Sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

Industry observers note that the most important part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

Hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Industry observers note that hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

It has been revealed that A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

According to recent reports, like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

Industry observers note that while cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

In a recent development, while all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Recent findings suggest that remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

In a recent development, remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!
  • Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval!
  • This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

For me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

Recent findings suggest that remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

For a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

Industry observers note that fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks says fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

Drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Recent findings suggest that warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

Dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Recent findings suggest that baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

She also writes about the latest gardening news and emerging trends, from pollinator-friendly planting to small-space edible gardens and sustainable outdoor living. When she’s not covering a viral moment, she’s cultivating her own love of gardening and bringing a storyteller’s eye to all things green and growing.

Breaking: It’s So Easy to Turn Your Garden Into An Owl Hangout – You Just Need 5 Plants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard.
  • The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.
  • According to recent reports, whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard. These mysterious nighttime visitors can be surprisingly elusive, but there are ways to make your garden a more welcoming place for them. And no, you don't need acres of woodland or a sprawling country estate to get your very own owl hangout started.

The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.

According to recent reports, whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey. And the good news? Well, you can make a surprisingly big difference with just five plants.

Sources indicate that that's right, folks! If you want more owls in your garden, that means providing shelter for small mammals, encouraging insects and other prey, and offering trees and shrubs where owls can perch, roost or potentially nest.

From tall native grasses to berry-producing shrubs and evergreen trees, then, these are some of the best additions for creating an owl-friendly backyard.

Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a fantastic native grass for an owl-friendly garden, particularly if you have a sunny spot where you can let it grow relatively undisturbed.

Why? Well, because its tall stems and dense clumps provide valuable cover for small mammals, including voles and mice, which are important prey for many owl species. The grass also offers shelter for other wildlife through winter, when more exposed parts of the garden can become less hospitable.

Switchgrass is particularly useful in meadow-style plantings, where it can grow alongside native wildflowers. It produces attractive seedheads in late summer and fall, too, and it's a relatively low-maintenance perennial once established.

According to recent reports, give it a sunny position and well-drained soil, then, and leave some of its growth standing over winter rather than cutting everything back in fall. You may just find it swiftly becomes your fresh favorite garden plant, let alone the best part of your owl hangout!

If you want to make your garden more appealing to owls, don't underestimate the value of evergreen trees! Native pines and spruces provide year-round cover, with dense branches offering potential daytime roosting spots and sheltered perches. Their evergreen foliage can also make wildlife feel more protected from disturbance and exposure.

Recent findings suggest that different owl species have different preferences, but trees are an crucial part of the habitat for many woodland-dwellers like barred owls. Some species also use natural cavities in mature trees for nesting.

If you have room, consider something like this stunning Eastern White Pine from Nature Hills. Just remember that a newly planted sapling is unlikely to become an instant owl retreat, though, so it's always better to preserve mature trees where you can!

A slightly wild patch of blackberry brambles (Rubus spp.) might not be everyone's idea of a perfectly manicured garden, but it's a genius addition to anyone hoping to turn their yard into an owl hangout. After all, blackberry thickets provide dense cover for small critters and nesting birds, not to mention food and shelter for plenty others besides.

Why does this matter for owls? Because a garden that supports a healthy range of small animals can help provide the prey that visiting owls need, of course! And you don't have to let blackberries take over your entire yard, either. A small patch of something like Baby Cakes® Blackberry Bush from Nature Hills along a boundary or at the back of a wildlife-friendly border can provide plenty of habitat value.

Just remember that brambles can spread, so give them room and keep growth away from paths and areas where people regularly walk.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) is a beautiful native shrub or small tree that brings several seasons of wildlife interest to the garden; think white flowers that attract pollinators, followed by edible berries in summer, which are enjoyed by birds and other wildlife.

In a recent development, its value doesn't stop with the berries; serviceberry also supports insects and provides useful woody cover, helping to create a more diverse backyard habitat. For an owl-friendly garden, this is all about supporting the wider food web... but hey, it helps that it's a stunner, too!

Industry observers note that goldenrod (Solidago spp.) is often overlooked as a wildlife plant, but its bright yellow flowers provide an important late-season source of nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies and other insects. Those insects, in turn, help support other wildlife, including small birds and mammals.

According to recent reports, some smaller owl species also eat large insects, making insect-rich habitats like goldenrod a must for your owl hangout! Especially as it's a lovely way to add late-summer and fall color to your garden. Many varieties are native to North America, and once established, they're generally easy to grow.

Something like the Fireworks Solidago (Goldenrod) Plant from Burpee is a great way to go!

In a recent development, these five plants are a great starting point for your owl hangout, but there are plenty of other native choices that can help make your backyard more wildlife-friendly. #.

Industry observers note that viburnums, for example, produce berries that feed birds and other wildlife, while their dense branching offers useful cover, too. Native dogwoods offer flowers, berries and dense branching that can provide shelter for wildlife, not to mention some much-added beauty to any yard (there's a reason they're swiftly replacing magnolias for a lot of people!).

Sources indicate that junipers offer dense year-round cover and provide berry-like cones that are eaten by birds and small mammals. And purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea) attract pollinators and produce seedheads that feed birds and other critters, too.

Of course, planting is a brilliant starting point, but there are a few other things you can do to make your garden more appealing to these fascinating birds. As ever, try leaving some areas of longer grass and natural vegetation rather than tidying every corner. Keep mature trees where possible, particularly those with natural cavities, and consider whether a species-appropriate owl nest box might be suitable for your local area.

In a recent development, it's also crucial to avoid rodent poisons, as owls can be exposed to rodenticides when they eat poisoned mice and rats. Keep lights to a minimum after the sun goes down, as they can confuse nocturnal birds and critters. And, finally, remember that owls need peace and quiet; take care to avoid disturbing potential roosting and nesting areas, particularly during breeding season.

You might not spot an owl straight away, but by planting for wildlife and allowing your garden to become a little more natural, you'll be creating a much richer habitat for all sorts of visitors. And who knows? Before too long, your owl hangout might just be the most buzzing nightspot in town...

Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

In this article, tech editor Mark Petersen discusses some aspects of deck building that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit plan review or site inspection. He focuses on building secure footings, ensuring proper ledger fastening, avoiding flashing mistakes, using correct connectors, and strengthening the framing.

In a recent development, I’ve built a lot of decks, some still standing after 30-plus years. I’ve also worked with several deck-building rock stars to create articles on the subject. I’ve even helped companies like Trex create a bunch of how-to content. In all my years of research and hands-on experience, I’ve seen plenty of examples of decks built to last.

On the flip side, I’ve come across structures that range from somewhat wobbly to absolutely unsafe due to feeble footings, poorly installed or absent ledger flashing, undersized framing, and missing or misused hardware and fasteners.

Building to code and following the requirements spelled out by your local building department will get you most of the way to a safe and durable deck, but even a code-compliant deck can be improved with some due diligence and attention to detail.

In this article, I’ve focused on some vulnerabilities that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit proposal review or site inspection. Think of this as an above-and-beyond checklist of details worth considering on your next deck build..

Industry observers note that drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

For years I worked for a production builder. They used to insulate a home’s rim-joist cavity with batt insulation and no vapor retarder, which was code-approved at the time. This caused all sorts of moisture damage from water vapor that was driven through the cavity.

Sources indicate that instead of switching to rigid or spray foam, their first fix was to install SIP rim joists, the most common of which have a core of EPS insulation sandwiched between OSB sheathing. This solution lasted less than a year because uninformed deck builders and homeowners assumed they could use standard lag screws to then attach deck ledgers to the rim joist.

The result was that most of those fasteners were secured to only the two layers of plywood that made up the SIP, rather than solid-sawn lumber—a serious problem when the connection is responsible for supporting the deck.

Sources indicate that so, don’t assume there’s a conventional solid-sawn rim joist behind the sheathing. The floor system might include an SIP rim joist or floor trusses with just a ribbon board instead of a solid ledger. When building a latest deck, a permit strategy review or site inspection will hopefully catch this, but if you are resurfacing an existing deck, now is the time to confirm a solid ledger connection.

According to recent reports, if you discover an SIP rim joist or a floor system that can’t support a conventional ledger connection, try to track down the manufacturer of the components in question for an approved attachment solution. If that’s not an option, you could consult an engineer or add a beam and posts near the house and build the deck as a freestanding structure.

Don’t attach a deck ledger to the rim joist of a cantilevered bump-out or bay window, or directly to a stud wall.

In a recent development, neither provides the load path assumed by conventional prescriptive ledger details. Nevertheless, this was common practice back in the day.

In fact, the ledger on my own son’s house is attached to a bay. A site inspection will likely catch this code violation, but if you are just making cosmetic improvements that don’t require a permit, do your due diligence.

In some cases, these connections can be made to work, but they typically require an engineered design and structural modifications, which might involve tearing into a finished ceiling to add blocking or other framing reinforcement. As with any questionable ledger connection, the simpler solution is to treat the deck as freestanding.

In a recent development, add a beam and posts close to the house so the deck loads are carried directly to footings rather than relying on a questionable ledger connection. That’s the fix I plan to make on my son’s house. In the meantime, I warned him against throwing any parties on the deck.

In my work as a contractor, I replaced several patio doors after either the door sill or ledger flashing failed, allowing water to rot the subfloor and some of the framing below it. I came across this problem primarily when deck boards were installed right up under the door sill, where splashing rain and melting Minnesota snow combined to wreak havoc over the years. To help prevent this, whenever possible I would install the deck a few inches below the door sill. I also instructed my customers to keep snow from piling up against the door.

Industry observers note that the main hurdle to installing a deck below the door sill is maintaining proper ledger-fastener placement. On a large deck, the ledger may be as deep as the house rim joist and dropping it a few inches can make it impossible to meet the required fastener edge distances in both the ledger and the rim joist. One solution is to use smaller deck joists and reduce their span by adding another beam. If this doesn’t work, you may need to consult an engineer for an alternative connection detail.

Of course, lowering the deck surface below the door sill isn’t as much of a concern in warm, dry regions—and it isn’t always an option when someone in the house has mobility challenges.

Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

In a recent development, the only deck callback I ever received happened after the first time I worked with composite fascia boards. I didn’t use enough fasteners. I thought the manufacturer’s recommended screw spacing was preposterous overkill, but I was wrong. The fascia buckled, and I returned to the scene, tail between my legs, to add more screws.

Sources indicate that in addition to protecting your reputation, following manufacturer recommendations can also preserve warranties. If you use unapproved fasteners or hidden clips on composite decking and there’s a factory defect, some companies might not stand behind their product. Most factory warranties stipulate using only approved installation methods and materials.

According to recent reports, double-check that the structural hardware you grab is rated for exterior use with the treated lumber you’re using. I nearly walked out of a home center with interior-grade joist hangers that were in the wrong bin. They looked almost identical to the exterior versions. Also, don’t mix stainless-steel and galvanized connectors and fasteners; dissimilar metals can accelerate corrosion.

Just as notable, use the fasteners specified by the connector manufacturer. Short hanger nails, roofing nails, deck screws, and whatever happens to be in your tool pouch aren’t necessarily acceptable substitutes. Pay particular attention to double-shear hangers: The angled fasteners often need to be longer than the face nails so they penetrate through the joist and well into the supporting member. And fill the required holes—structural hardware only provides its rated capacity when it’s installed the way it was tested.

For comprehensive info on deck hardware, including fastener and hardware options and how each connection works to keep the deck structure intact, check out Mike Guertin’s video series, “Critical Deck-Framing Connections.”.

#158988. Bringing Your Citrus Trees Indoors for Winter? Get These 6 Things Right to Avoid Leaf Drop and Pests

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Bringing Your Citrus Trees Indoors for Winter? Get These 6 Things Right to Avoid Leaf Drop and Pests

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun.
  • Industry observers note that the move itself is a shock, though.
  • In a recent development, that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun. Then the cold arrives. Citrus can't take a hard freeze, so in colder climates, potted trees have to come inside for winter.

Industry observers note that the move itself is a shock, though. Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after. Indoor light is weaker, the air is drier, and pests that rode in on the branches can spread to nearby houseplants.

In a recent development, that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike. Six checks before the tree comes through the door can head off much of that.

Recent findings suggest that most citrus can be damaged below 32°F (0°C), and a potted tree is more exposed than one in the ground. Lemons and limes are usually the most tender, while kumquats, satsumas, and calamondins can handle a little more chill. Aim to have the tree inside before nights start dipping into the 40s (4–9°C). Wait for the first freeze warning, and you'll be dragging a heavy pot from full sun straight indoors. Give it a week or two in a shady spot near the house first instead – it adjusts to lower light that way.

Flip the leaves over and look along the midvein. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) highlights up there as small, flat, tan bumps. Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) leave pale speckles and, eventually, fine webbing where the leaf meets the stem, and white, cottony clumps in the leaf joints usually mean citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri).

Recent findings suggest that if you find anything, spray the tree outdoors with an insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil labeled for citrus, such as Monterey horticultural oil concentrate. Plan on more than one round. Once inside, keep it away from other houseplants for three or four weeks.

Bugs don't only ride in on the leaves. Tip the pot on its side, look in the drainage holes, and lift the saucer. Slugs, sowbugs, and earwigs all like that damp spot underneath, and ants sometimes leave small piles of potting mix they've hauled out. A slow soak with the hose drives many of them out.

In a recent development, check any roots poking through the holes, too. Firm, light-colored roots are a good sign, but dark, mushy ones and a sour smell point to waterlogged soil. Unless the roots are in real trouble, wait to repot citrus trees until spring.

According to recent reports, citrus needs far more light than a pothos or snake plant. Indoors, aim for at least six hours of bright light a day. A south- or southwest-facing window is usually the best spot, with the tree close to the glass but not touching it. Up north, short winter days often fall short – that's when a grow light helps. Glowrium sells a dual-head LED grow light on Amazon that's just under 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, with heads that bend toward the canopy. Trees moved from full sun to a dim corner overnight often shed a good share of their leaves.

Recent findings suggest that hold a hand over a heating vent or radiator when the heat kicks on. That hot, dry air blows straight across the leaves of a nearby tree, and a cold, drafty window or door is no better. Sudden swings like those commonly trigger leaf drop. Somewhere around 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night, about 55–65°F (13–18°C), works well.

Humidity near 50% helps in a heated house. The Pure Enrichment MistAire humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours on a tank, and the ThermoPro digital hygrometer can sit by the pot to track both.

Sources indicate that on a hot patio, potted citrus can need water every day or two. Indoors, with cooler rooms and less light, it uses much less, and the summer routine can drown the roots. Push a finger about 2 inches (5 cm) into the mix, and water only when it feels dry at that depth. Deep pots are harder to judge, which is where a moisture meter, like the Xlux Long Probe Plant Soil Moisture Meter, is invaluable.

It has been revealed that water until some drains out, then empty the saucer. Set the pot on a few terra-cotta Pot Toes to keep the drainage holes clear. Don't overcorrect, though – a tree left bone dry for long stretches drops flowers and can lose leaves.

In a recent development, some leaf drop in the first few weeks is common. Less light, drier air, and new temperatures all hit at once, and a few leaves on the floor are just part of it, mostly.

Sources indicate that look closer if leaves keep falling after the first month or whole branches go bare. A wet, sour-smelling mix points to overwatering, while a mix that's dry all the way down means it went too long between drinks. Check how close the tree sits to a vent or cold door, and whether that window is as bright in December as it seemed in October. Sticky spots, webbing, or cottony clumps under the leaves mean pests got past the quarantine.

Get through those six checks, and your tree has an easier winter ahead. Come spring, once nights stay above 50°F (10°C), it can head back out to the patio a little at a time.

His growing success highlights that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#158987. This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1043 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective.
  • Sources indicate that pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones.
  • We all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective. It’s so disappointing when a Schlumbergera isn’t showing even the smallest pinpricks of colored buds on its stem ends by late fall, especially if you’ve been diligently delivering all the care your Christmas cactus needs in November. But by shifting your stubborn plant into survival mode, you can kickstart its bloom cycle. And guess what? All you need is a banana and a plastic bag.

Sources indicate that pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones. This causes the plants to stop growing green leaf segments and switch to developing flowerbuds. And you can use the exact same idea with the natural chemicals a ripe banana releases if your Christmas cactus isn't blooming yet.

We all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast. That’s down to the ethylene it emits, a natural hormone that plants release when nearing the end of their life cycle. So, by trapping ethylene around your Christmas cactus for a short time, you can trick the plant into thinking it’s under extreme threat, which triggers it to develop flowers as a last-ditch survival effort to preserve its genetics via seed production. Clever, huh?

Highly ripe bananas that have brown spots or are turning brown emit the highest levels of ethylene. You only need to use the peel: though the whole fruit produces ethylene gas, the soft, sweet flesh of a banana is a magnet for fruit flies and fungus gnats and adds too much moisture to the little greenhouse you’re about to create.

Excess moisture will swiftly evaporate from the inner surface of the peel, further reducing humidity and any risk of pests or disease.

Now stand your Christmas cactus, still in its container, on a plate or big plant saucer and lay the banana peel alongside the pot base. It’s important that the peel doesn’t touch the leaf segments or soil as this risks transferring mold or fungal spores.

Recent findings suggest that pull a clear plastic bag down over the plant, plate and banana peel, and tuck or tie under the plate to seal. If the bag is flimsy and falls onto the stems, use chopsticks or skewers poked into the soil to create a frame so there's no direction contact between plant and plastic.

It’s vital the bag is clear as an opaque bag is likely to take the stress a step too far and your plant may drop leaf segments instead of developing buds. It also means you can keep a close eye on your plant through the process. A clear unscented trash bag like this from Amazon is ideal as it's plenty major enough to make fashioning your mini-greenhouse easy.

Now your Christmas cactus is in its little greenhouse, it’ll swiftly overheat if it’s hit by the sun’s rays so find it a spot in a bright room but out of direct sunlight.

The optimum amount of time to leave your Schlumbergera in its ethylene tank is exactly 2 days and 2 nights. This gives the gas plenty of time to chemically shock the plant and trigger bud development, without damaging the plant or giving mold a chance to develop in the restricted air circulation.

In a recent development, while professional growers use incredibly precise parts-per-million doses of synthetic chemicals, you can’t tell exactly how much ethylene your chosen banana is emitting. So, keep an eye on your Christmas cactus and if at any point the plant looks like it’s struggling or there’s the slightest sign of mold, remove the bag straight away. Don’t be tempted to leave the bag on any longer than 48 hours as too much ethylene can harm bud development.

Recent findings suggest that carefully take off the plastic bag, discard the peel and place your plant in the spot where you want it to flower, being sure to avoid these Christmas cactus disaster zones. After a week or so, you should see pinhead-sized bumps starting to form on the leaf segment tips and by two weeks, they should be clearly visible.

It’s vital you check your plant hasn’t already begun developing buds before trying this trick. Inspect leaf tips under a bright light – or use a cheap magnifying glass with LED light like this from Amazon – to look for any bumps beginning to form right on the tips of the leaf segments. These may be tiny so gently feel for them with a fingertip, too. If your Schlumbergera has pink or red flowers these little bumps will be bright but if your plant blooms white they may be green and harder to spot.

Industry observers note that if you’re in any doubt, wait a week and see if those bumps get any bigger. While using ethylene from ripe banana peel is a very effective way to get a Christmas cactus to flower, this hormone shock can also cause existing buds to stall if the process has already begun.

If this pro growers' trick doesn’t work, there’s likely an underlying reason why your Christmas cactus isn't flowering, that’s overriding the plant’s system.

The banana bag trick is well worth trying if your Christmas cactus doesn’t have buds yet, and you still just have enough time to trigger your plant into producing flowers for the holidays. Next year, be sure to use the black-out hack that tricks your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time, and you won’t have to worry!

She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

Meet The Christmas Tree That Flowers In Summer – This Stunning Evergreen Puts On A Spectacular Display

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you think of a Christmas tree, chances are you picture a familiar fir or spruce, perhaps decorated with twinkling lights and festive ornaments. But, for some people, Christmas looks a little different.

Sources indicate that that's right; instead of bringing an evergreen indoors, many people celebrate the season beneath a spectacular flowering tree covered in brilliant red blooms. Meet the Latest Zealand Christmas Tree, also known as the pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). This extraordinary evergreen puts on one of the most eye-catching floral displays of summer, transforming coastlines and gardens with masses of vibrant crimson flowers.

And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...

Shop Flowering Christmas Trees:.

It has been revealed that native to Latest Zealand, the pōhutukawa has earned its festive nickname thanks to its spectacular flowering season, which coincides with Christmas in the Southern Hemisphere. Because, while much of the northern hemisphere is welcoming winter with bare branches and chilly temperatures, New Zealand is enjoying the height of summer... and that's when this remarkable tree really comes into its own.

Recent findings suggest that rather than having conventional petals, its unmistakable flowers look just like fluffy red brushes (which pollinators love). And, against the tree's glossy green leaves, the effect is nothing short of spectacular.

A post shared by Hahana (@hahana_official).

Although it can reach around 65 feet tall in its natural habitat, younger New Zealand Christmas trees can be grown from seed in large containers (although they need plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil and protection from frost).

According to recent reports, for US gardeners, growing one outdoors will generally be limited to warmer and frost-free USDA Zones, so it isn't necessarily a practical choice for everyone. Luckily, though, there are other flowering evergreens that can deliver a similarly spectacular effect...

If it's the striking crimson display of the pōhutukawa that catches your eye, bottlebrush is perhaps the closest alternative when it comes to finding a flowering evergreen that might serve well as a Christmas tree. Especially as its bright red blooms have plenty in common with the Kiwi native.

Depending on the variety and climate, bottlebrush (available at Walmart) can flower from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. Many varieties are evergreen and container-friendly, too, although they prefer a sunny position and well-drained soil.

For gardeners who love the idea of a flowering Christmas tree, but prefer something with more traditional-looking blooms, southern magnolia is a beautiful option, as its enormous (and fabulously fragranced) flowers can measure up to 12 inches across.

While it doesn't have the bright red flowers of the pōhutukawa, it shares some of its most appealing qualities: year-round evergreen foliage, a substantial tree-like presence and an impressive summer floral display. For smaller spaces, consider a compact cultivar such as this 'Little Gem' from Expert Gardener. It has a naturally narrower growth habit than many full-sized southern magnolias, making it a more manageable choice for smaller gardens.

It can also be grown in a large container so long as you treat it to sufficient room, good drainage and consistent moisture.

If fragrance is just as key as appearance, gardenia is another gorgeous Christmas tree alternative thanks to its deep-green foliage and exquisite white flowers.

Sources indicate that oh sure, their blooms may be smaller than those of the southern magnolia, but they more than make up for it with their intoxicating perfume. And, as they don't naturally grow into large trees, standard-trained gardenias can make particularly attractive container garden options; generally best suited to warmer USDA growing zones, growing them in pots makes it easier to protect them from cold weather.

Something like the Frost Proof Gardenia from Nature Hills is happily able to handle temperatures down to 0-10°F, too!

The Latest Zealand Christmas Tree is a wonderful reminder that evergreens don't have to be all about foliage; indeed, some of the most spectacular trees and shrubs combine year-round greenery with extraordinary seasonal flowers.

According to recent reports, whether you choose the fiery red blooms of bottlebrush, the impressive flowers of southern magnolia or the beautiful fragrance of gardenia, there's no shortage of ways to bring that flowering-evergreen look into your own garden. And who knows? You might even find yourself looking at your Christmas tree traditions a little differently as a result...

Sources indicate that kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend aims to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#158983. How to Spot a Houseplant With Spider Mites – and Prayer Plants are #1 Victims This Month

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

How to Spot a Houseplant With Spider Mites – and Prayer Plants are #1 Victims This Month

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves.
  • Industry observers note that as soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive.
  • Sources indicate that spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves. While spider mites can target any houseplant, prayer plants are the most commonly affected, with monstera and alocasia close behind. So, if you're disappointed to discover some houseplant leaves fading, looking dusty or appearing speckled with tiny spots at this time of year, don’t presume it's just dust: check to see if your houseplant has spider mites straight away.

Industry observers note that as soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive. The time it takes for these pests to reproduce reduces as temperatures rise, and in cozy conditions a single spider mite can turn into a thousand in a couple of weeks. Which is why, when mid-November arrives, numbers suddenly explode and we start spotting spider-mite infestations in houseplants.

Sources indicate that spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too. These common houseplant pests can be easily managed, though, and the earlier you catch the problem, the easier it is to deal with. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a spider mite infestation.

First, rule out dust by wiping the houseplant's leaves with a soft, damp cloth. Then look for these signs that signal you could be dealing with a spider mite infestation:.

Recent findings suggest that spider mites are actually arachnids, like spiders, not mites. They are extremely small – about a half a millimeter – and generally gather on the undersides of leaves. Here they pierce the leaves and suck out the contents to feed. The resulting damage from these feeding spots are very small, pale dots on the tops of foliage that can’t be wiped away, and these speckled leaves are a tell-tale sign of an infestation. As the population of spider mites grows, you’ll start to see fine silk webbing, which can easily be mistaken for dusty houseplant leaves.

Houseplants with broad, thin leaves that are easy to pierce are the most favored. While prayer plants are the most commonly attacked, monstera, alocasia, ficus, croton, palms, English ivy and dracaena are also highly susceptible to these pests.

Industry observers note that early intervention is the key to success if you have a houseplant with a spider mite infestation. But, even if you're dealing with a heavy infestation, these steps will work, though you'll need to repeat them to break the spider mite lifecycle.

Industry observers note that it's vital to keep the affected plant away from other houseplants as spider mites can easily move from one plant to another. Move it to a different, plant-free room until the problem has been resolved. Now that you know what to look for, check all your other houseplants very carefully for early, subtle signs of an infestation.

Next, you want to get rid of as many of the mites as you can. The easiest way to do this is to place your houseplant in the shower or bathtub and give it a good rinse. Use a firm stream of water so the pressure rinses most of the pests off, but ensure the jet isn't so harsh that it damages the plant.

In a recent development, be sure to direct the water to the undersides of leaves where the mites are feeding and at any webbing you can see. Follow the rinse with a thorough wiping with a damp cloth to remove any webbing still attached. This process is unlikely to remove all the mites or their eggs, so repeat the process every few days as fresh eggs hatch.

Industry observers note that regular rinsing reduces a spider mite population but it doesn't remove it entirely. To fully break the lifecycle, you'll need an insecticidal soap with a natural formula such as NatureStop Insecticidal Soap, available from Amazon, or a neem oil spray like Captain Jack's Need Oil Spray for Plants, also on Amazon. These organic options will treat indoor plant pests safely. Insecticidal soap kills mites on contact by breaking down their cell membranes, while neem oil disrupts feeding and reproduction and smothers pests.

Follow the label instructions for whichever product you choose and be sure to cover all areas of the plant, including undersides of leaves and stems. This is important as both products work by direct contact with the mites. Repeat the application as often as suggested on the label, as you’ll likely need several applications to get rid of pests completely.

Remove any badly damaged leaves, whether they're heavily stippled, have turned mostly yellow or have brown, crispy areas. Snip off with sharp pruners and dispose of them in the garbage (not the compost). Any foliage that's mostly green can be left and, while damaged leaves won’t return to their former glory, healthy areas will still photosynthesize and support the plant’s recovery.

Good houseplant care in fall will make conditions less favorable to spider mites:.

Industry observers note that if houseplant leaves have irregular patches of white or light gray powder on their surfaces that can be wiped away, this is likely a fungal infection, powdery mildew and should be treated by disposing of heavily affected leaves and using a product like neem oil or a commercial houseplant fungicide. A white film or larger spots could be mineral deposits from watering If you have hard water and mist or irrigate houseplants from above, easily fixed by cleaning leaves then avoiding getting foliage wet.

#158981. Latest Update: Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

Latest Update: Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass.
  • Recent findings suggest that fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder.
  • In a recent development, this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

Recent findings suggest that fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

In a recent development, this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

Many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

Recent findings suggest that it’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

Instead of endlessly raking, run a mulching mower, like this Greenworks model, over the grass as needed, chopping up the leaves when you see light to moderate coverage. Another option is to remove some of a thick layer of leaves for use in compost or as a mulch in beds. Don’t worry about removing every last leaf before winter.

Recent findings suggest that fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

Industry observers note that A simple rain gauge, such as this easy-to-read JMBay model from Amazon, can help you keep track of rainfall. Keep an eye on the soil and rain and decide when the grass could use a deep drink rather than sticking with a strict schedule.

Of course, there are exceptions. If you have seeded parts of the lawn or installed upcoming sod before winter, these areas should be watered regularly right up until the ground freezes.

At some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but plan to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

It has been revealed that keep mowing to the recommended height for your type of grass until the final cut. A tool like the Oregon Deck Leveling Gauge from Amazon can help you check your mower's cutting height and ensure an even cut.

As growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

Sources indicate that bagging all of your healthy grass clippings is unnecessary. It’s also a highly labor-intensive chore. Don’t waste your time, energy, or back on this one. Finely chopped grass decomposes rapidly and adds nutrients to the soil. And, contrary to popular belief, grass clippings left on the ground do not contribute to thatch buildup.

In a recent development, instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer significant clumps you'll get.

Managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

Industry observers note that instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

According to recent reports, fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

Cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

It has been revealed that your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

Industry observers note that instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

According to recent reports, as you blueprint fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#158980. Breaking: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2427 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems.
  • For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics.
  • Sources indicate that my company, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems. Plenum trusses create dedicated spaces above ceilings for ductwork and other mechanical systems within the home’s conditioned envelope, helping maintain consistent ceiling heights while improving energy efficiency and durability. Successful implementation requires early coordination among builders, architects, HVAC designers, and truss manufacturers, along with carefully planned duct layouts and continuous, airtight control layers to prevent moisture problems and ensure long-term performance.

For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics. The wide-open, easy-to-access attic space makes the practice common, convenient, and familiar for the framing and mechanical trades. But from a building-performance standpoint, it’s a terrible idea. Vented attics are extremely hot in summer and cold in winter, so every foot of duct placed in that location exposes the conditioned air within the ductwork to temperatures way beyond those inside the house.

Sources indicate that my company, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now. We have a hot, humid climate and—like in many places—attic ductwork is common here, so we’ve seen plenty of examples of what can happen when you install HVAC equipment in an unconditioned space.

For starters, the extreme temperature difference between the conditioned air inside the ducts and the temperature outside them results in a house that uses more energy and is more expensive to heat and cool compared to a house with an HVAC system inside the conditioned space. And the additional expense isn’t limited to operational costs. HVAC ducts and equipment in unconditioned spaces must have higher capacities to compensate for the adverse conditions where they’re located, meaning the systems are more expensive.

In a recent development, higher costs are not the only downsides. Supply and return air leaks are common with HVAC systems in attics and are problematic from a building-durability and performance perspective. Supply leaks waste conditioned air and pressurize the attic, which depressurizes the house, causing additional air leakage in the conditioned space—and in extreme scenarios, backdrafting of combustion appliances.

Sources indicate that backdrafting can release carbon monoxide into the home, creating a serious risk of poisoning. There’s also a lot of water vapor in flue gasses, which can create humidity problems and mold growth. Equally common are return leaks that pull dusty, humid, or hot attic air into the heating or cooling system, negatively affecting energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and indoor air quality.

Sources indicate that air-conditioning supply ducts, which are cold, often become condensing surfaces. Condensing water can ruin finishes and lead to mold growth that may or may not be visible. Mold you can’t see can be especially problematic for sensitive individuals who might experience cold-like symptoms, asthma, or other respiratory problems. Similar problems can occur in cold climates when warm, conditioned air contacts cold spaces, creating condensation and potential mold problems. Even the most reliable HVAC system, when located outside the enclosure, can lead to comfort complaints and callbacks that are hard to diagnose and fix.

Recent findings suggest that you can avoid all these problems by making room for HVAC ducts inside the house’s conditioned space during the design phase, before the house is built. The concept is not latest—building scientists started advocating for ductwork within conditioned spaces in the late ’80s and early ’90s, and conscientious builders and designers paid attention. They developed methods for hiding ductwork in dropped hallway ceilings and in soffits that run along the tops of walls (see the drawings).

These methods work—but from a design perspective, employing them can be tough on some homes. I’ve found that soffits in bedrooms are almost always unwanted by designers and clients. I think the best way to hide ducts, both significant and small, is to place them in ceiling chases using plenum trusses.

It has been revealed that my first exposure to plenum trusses came from architect Steve Baczek. For a period, Steve was working with a production builder in the Southwest United States that offered a comfort guarantee for every home they built. One of the ways they ensured comfort was by keeping the HVAC system inside the building envelope. In some parts of the house, Steve hid ductwork in soffits, but he also used plenum trusses in places where soffits were impractical. The idea of using plenum trusses stuck with me.

It has been revealed that we eventually began using plenum trusses in some of our builds for the same reasons as Steve: greater comfort, efficiency, and building durability. In 2017, our tech giant made the decision that ductwork and HVAC equipment would be installed inside the conditioned enclosure whenever possible. In homes with a conditioned attic, the solution is easy. The ducts can simply live in the attic. The same is true when we have a conditioned crawlspace or basement available for distribution.

In a recent development, many of the homes we build, however, are slab-on-grade with a vented attic above them. Those homes require another strategy, and plenum trusses have become one of our preferred solutions. They allow us to maintain consistent ceiling heights throughout the house while still providing a dedicated space for ductwork and other mechanical systems inside the building envelope. The result gives us the architectural appearance we want without compromising the mechanical strategy, occupant comfort, or energy efficiency.

Plenum trusses are engineered with an open space free of chords and braces that becomes a cavity for ducts, pipes, and refrigeration lines running perpendicular to the trusses. This plenum cavity is lined with an air-impermeable material, typically wood sheathing or drywall for airtightness. Ducts can also be run in angled plenums or in an airtight plenum space made between two trusses, as seen in the photos below.

Sources indicate that parallel Plenum: In this space, eight girder trusses have an opening that allows a duct to pass through them and then turn 90° into a plenum space built on-site from taped sheathing between two of the girder trusses. Both site-built and engineered plenum spaces need a continuous air barrier—in this case, taped sheathing—to prevent air movement through the plenum space.

Angled Plenum: To get the conditioned air to its intended registers most efficiently, the main plenum on this project is angled and installed within 10 individually engineered trusses. Each truss has the plenum space offset a few inches from the previous truss’s plenum space, creating the angled plenum. It took about an hour with the truss designer to plan this layout.

Strapped Ceiling: Once the ductwork is installed and sealed and other mechanicals are in place, the ceiling is strapped with 2×4 furring for securing the finished drywall ceiling.

A plenum truss offers a way to design a house’s framing around the mechanical systems, rather than squeezing ductwork into whatever leftover space is available. In simple terms, the bottom chord of a plenum truss is notched with a framed rectangle above, creating a dedicated service cavity, or chase, above the finished ceiling. Importantly, the chase is within the building enclosure, beneath the air, insulation, and vapor control layers—unlike an unconditioned attic, which is essentially outside the building. In addition to ductwork, the plenum space can also house electrical and low-voltage wiring, pipes, and other mechanical systems while keeping them inside the conditioned space of the home.

The notable point is that the chase is designed, not discovered. You can’t build the chase with field alterations after the trusses arrive. By then, the rooflines, heel heights, load paths, bearing points, ceiling planes, and mechanical layout are already largely locked in. A plenum-truss strategy can only work when the builder, architect, mechanical designer, and truss supplier are involved early on and work together. In my experience, the biggest challenge has been the truss design. Nearly every builder or designer I know who uses plenum trusses has encountered some degree of resistance or hesitation from a truss manufacturer, which I think is understandable. We are asking the truss designer to create something more complicated than a conventional roof truss while accommodating structural loads, duct dimensions, roof geometry, bearing locations, and the other constraints of the building.

The best results we have had come from working directly with the truss designer early in the process. Whenever possible, we sit down with the designer and work through the layout before the trusses are finalized. An extra hour spent with a truss designer is how you end up with a plenum large enough to fit and efficiently route the ducts while framing the complicated rooflines typical of the custom homes we build. Modern truss-design software makes it relatively easy to look at the proposed truss geometry and determine if the plenum will be major enough and correctly positioned for efficiently routing ducts that are the right size.

Plenum ceilings use furred-down framing or drywall-suspension systems to lower the entire ceiling. The system requires a second air barrier above the furred-down section(s), adding significant cost and complexity to the whole ceiling assembly and not just the plenum service cavity.

Sources indicate that lowered ceilings refer to a section of lowered ceiling (often in hallways), and were pioneered by building scientists as a way to keep ductwork in the conditioned space. The system is less expensive than dropping an entire ceiling, but many clients find the lowered portion of ceiling makes the hallway or other space feel oppressive or confining.

Wall-to-ceiling soffits provide a space between the ceiling and the top of built-in cabinetry. Unfortunately, the design is often limited to concealing small ducts, and clients and designers often object to soffits outside the kitchen, especially when they obstruct a view or look like an afterthought.

Conditioned attics bring the insulation, air-control, and vapor-control layers to the roof sheathing, typically with spray foam on the underside of the roof sheathing. But insulating an entire attic with spray foam is expensive, and conditioned attics add a lot of space that must be temperature-controlled, increasing costs over time.

Industry observers note that once the house design is finalized, the next step is to determine where the ducts and equipment need to go. That means the HVAC design must be figured out before the trusses are ordered. The air-handler location, trunk lines, branch runs, register locations, return ducts, and grilles need to be finalized during the design process. A real duct layout matters. A rectangular box on a plan marked “mechanical” is not enough, so we engage our mechanical design team early in the process and make sure the duct size and routing is specified in their HVAC design. Leaving the duct sizing and routing to whoever reveals up on installation day is never the right approach.

Once the duct layout is understood, the truss designer can design the truss framing to accommodate it. The chase needs to be deep and wide enough for the ductwork and anything else other trades require in the plenum space. It also needs to provide reasonable access for the people doing the work. If a duct must be bent, crushed, or forced around a framing member, the truss and/or HVAC design has failed. This is where builders need to be assertive in preconstruction. It’s not enough to simply ask whether the ductwork will fit—the HVAC designers should be able to identify on the looks where it will fit. By the end of the design process, the framing plan, mechanical plan, and truss drawings must agree with one another.

A plenum truss only improves building and HVAC performance if the service cavity is within the home’s conditioned enclosure, without any gaps in the control layers. The air-barrier location has to be clear, which can be verified using what building scientist Joe Lstiburek and architect Steve Baczek describe as the “red pen test.” You should be able to trace the home’s entire air barrier location on the plans without lifting a red pen. If the ceiling drywall is the primary air barrier and vapor-control layer, then the plenum needs to be detailed so the ceiling drywall connects to the drywall or sheathing surrounding the plenum cavity, keeping the air- and vapor-control layers continuous. In most cases, this means the plenum is drywalled inside, ducts are installed and sealed, and then ceiling drywall is installed below the plenum, creating a flat ceiling with hidden ductwork above.

We use Zip System sheathing as our air control layer in the plenum space and on the rest of the building enclosure. Our framing crews install and tape the sheathing in the plenum space as part of their framing contract. The material might cost a little more than a drywall air barrier, but we find that having the framers install the air barrier works better with job sequencing than having the drywallers at the project twice, first to install and tape the plenum drywall and a second time to drywall the rest of the house. Whether you use drywall or taped sheathing, the takeaway is the same: All three sides (sides and cap) of the plenum, and where it meets the ceiling drywall, must be airtight.

Recent findings suggest that the enclosure must also be airtight for vapor control, as most water that condenses on building surfaces and in cavities leading to mold and damage is the result of water vapor carried by air leaks that condenses on cold surfaces. Condensation can occur if the plenum space is not properly sealed from air movement, so you need a continuous air control layer in the plenum space and throughout the rest of the building for effective air and vapor control.

There’s no question that plenum trusses require more preconstruction planning than installing ducts and air handlers in unvented attics, and they typically add to the cost of a truss package. But the upfront planning and additional costs should be weighed against the cost of comfort complaints, wasted energy dollars, mold risk, and the labor involved with sealing penetrations and insulating ducts and HVAC equipment in unvented attics. Keeping ducts and HVAC equipment out of unconditioned spaces makes longer-lasting, more comfortable houses, which makes the additional effort and expense a smart investment for our clients.

— Jake Bruton is the president of Aarow Builders in Columbia, Mo. Photos by the author. Drawings by Dan Thornton.

Breaking: November Is the Perfect Time to Plant These 6 Fruit Trees – You'll Enjoy Delicious Harvests for Years

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow
