💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away.
  • That's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree!
  • Industry observers note that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

That's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

Industry observers note that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”. Is it any wonder, then, that when the interior designer shared a video of her Christmas decor to Instagram, the blooms were front and center?

A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco).

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

Industry observers note that it's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Shop Shea McGee-Inspired Christmas Decor:.

Keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

Cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”.

It has been revealed that flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

Recent findings suggest that timing is highly important as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

Sources indicate that when it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories claims, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”.

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

The best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

In a recent development, there’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. One massive bunch at the top looks like a mistake.”.

Sources indicate that arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and says to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

For McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”.

Dried petals shed, which is why Melam is so blunt with their advice: “You lose petals every time you touch a flower.” Cameron’s fix is a light hairspray mist that “keeps the shedding down.” And, as for those annoying relatives, who “just want to adjust one thing,” tell them that your Shea McGee-inspired Christmas tree is now a museum exhibit, so hands off".

According to recent reports, if you don't have real hydrangeas in your yard, faux hydrangeas as a no-mess alternative. These cream-white stems give the same soft look without the shedding.

Hydrangeas are also toxic if chewed, so keep clusters out of reach of curious pets.

Recent findings suggest that those candles on Shea McGee’s Christmas tree? Make them LED.

Melam notes, “Open flame is a no-no since the dry material will ignite right away.” As for saving them for next year, the experts are once again split.

Want a warm glow like MsGee's but without the fire risk? These warm white, dimmable clip-on LED candles come with a remote, so you can keep real flames far from your dried hydrangeas.

It has been revealed that melam stores heads flat in a box with tissue between layers, and Cameron has reused the same heads two years running. However, McFarland claims dried blooms “won’t do particularly well in storage” and suggests composting them and cutting fresh ones.

Either way, it’s a good excuse to plant more hydrangeas and see what tip works best for you.

#158956. Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2366 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
  • According to recent reports, my first response is usually that this is a good thing.
  • But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

According to recent reports, my first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a company where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

Industry observers note that the phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the tech giant wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

According to recent reports, those are the moments when someone usually says, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

According to recent reports, sit across the table with an experienced builder and you quickly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction firm live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

Before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the company to look like in five years? And—just as notable—what do they want less of?

Sources indicate that that last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

Industry observers note that I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a company different becomes clear.

At this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

If you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

Industry observers note that then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere new, that kind of focus becomes even more notable.

For example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the firm looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

In some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

Recent findings suggest that so Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned new builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

Industry observers note that if the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your company well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly update your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

Be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

What made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

How did each of those projects find you?

Maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

Who is connected to the work you want?

According to recent reports, make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

How can you stay connected to those people?

In a recent development, could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

Do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

Sources indicate that this is usually the point where someone claims, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

Then pay attention to what happens. Ask every latest caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

According to recent reports, for example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

In fact, when we started talking about where he wants the tech giant to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his company valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

The goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

Sources indicate that when I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the organization does “quality construction.”.

If you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of concerns, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

Bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the manufacturer does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels demonstrated more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

Becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something fresh. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

According to recent reports, I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

Sources indicate that A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

Once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your company visible.

Recent findings suggest that and there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your company also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

Sources indicate that make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

— Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

#158953. What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say.
  • Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right.
  • According to recent reports, take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

According to recent reports, take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Industry observers note that don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

Sources indicate that if you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

It has been revealed that low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

Recent findings suggest that on a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

Recent findings suggest that ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

Tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Recent findings suggest that winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward fresh growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

Recent findings suggest that don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Industry observers note that run the same five checks again around the latest year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

7 Thanksgiving Scraps to Save for Backyard Birds – Give Them a Helping Hand This Holiday

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they?
  • Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).
  • Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

The trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

Have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

Cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

Recent findings suggest that cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Industry observers note that frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

It has been revealed that pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

Take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

Cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil quickly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

Leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

Sources indicate that P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

In a recent development, A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

In a recent development, please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

Sources indicate that it's every bit as key to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid quickly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

It has been revealed that once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

Take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Margo Valdes, Weatherization Contractor

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science.
  • Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England.
  • Recent findings suggest that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science. Three years ago, she founded Athena Building Performance, a weatherization tech giant built on the premise that getting the details right starts with understanding why a building behaves the way it does.

Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England. The class explored how to determine the age of a castle, identify the type of stone used to build it, and understand the reasoning behind its design. Margo loved it.

Recent findings suggest that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult). The job sounded like a good fit, so she applied, and her career in building performance began.

Margo spent about six years at CSG and credits the company with giving her a strong foundation in building science. Though her work as a HERS rater focused on testing and evaluating, she received hands-on training in air-sealing and choosing and installing insulation. After leaving CSG, Margo’s focus shifted from latest construction to existing buildings. She joined a consulting firm, where she spent seven years as director of the Existing Buildings team.

According to recent reports, over the years, Margo became increasingly aware of how much the quality of weatherization work depends on understanding the building as a system—adding insulation affects moisture, and sealing air leaks changes ventilation. She decided the best way to improve the work was to get closer to it. That led her to the contractor side of the business, and to founding Athena.

According to recent reports, today, Athena operates as a specialized weatherization contractor, tackling residential air-sealing and insulation upgrades. While Margo spends most of her time managing the business, knowledgeable practice remains at its heart: Every new hire spends weeks doing hands-on field training and diagnostic walk-throughs to understand not just how the work is done, but why.

Margo envisions eventually expanding Athena into a full-service building-enclosure firm. For now, she’s focused on centering the firm around what started it all: thoughtful, educated work.

Breaking: Dissolving Into the Forest

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This home was designed with two main goals in mind.
  • Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.
  • Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

Spring Returns to Ezequiel’s Cottage Garden in Argentina

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December.
  • I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North.
  • According to recent reports, plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another patch as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

According to recent reports, plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a major hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

A view of the backyard perennial beds.

Purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

Sources indicate that this massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

In a recent development, another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something upcoming to discover just about everywhere!

Thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

To submit, fill out the Garden Photo of the Day Submission Form.

In a recent development, you can also send 5–10 photos to [email protected] along with some information about the plants in the pictures and where you took the photos. We’d love to hear where you are located, how long you’ve been gardening, successes you are proud of, failures you learned from, hopes for the future, favorite plants, or funny stories from your garden.

#158942. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2227 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers.
  • In a recent development, as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses.
  • Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

In a recent development, as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.

Successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Recent findings suggest that growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

Containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

Industry observers note that it’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more quickly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

Recent findings suggest that one advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

It has been revealed that because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Sources indicate that mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

Sources indicate that the ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the massive-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

It has been revealed that not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

In a recent development, are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

Industry observers note that when composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

While incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also key to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

In a recent development, A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Sources indicate that another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

Sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

Industry observers note that by definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

Don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a upcoming life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you proposal to harvest from them.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

In a recent development, some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you proposal to leave them in place for a second season.

Sources indicate that osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Industry observers note that another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Industry observers note that lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Recent findings suggest that vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

It has been revealed that alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Sources indicate that peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

In a recent development, and there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

Sources indicate that they also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a upcoming focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

According to recent reports, in the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

Heather Tuckman is a garden designer and owner of Resilient Ground Design in southeastern Pennsylvania. She combines her background in horticulture, garden design, and psychology to create beautiful, ecologically thoughtful landscapes.

Tech Report: Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day.
  • It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation.
  • With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Industry observers note that finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Sources indicate that hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Industry observers note that another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

In a recent development, patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, upcoming pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is key to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Industry observers note that repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

In a recent development, it’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

In a recent development, whether you’re planning a newly introduced patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

Mark Dwyer owns Landscape Prescriptions by MD and is the garden manager for the Edgerton Hospital Healing Garden in Edgerton, Wisconsin. He previously served as director of horticulture at Rotary Botanical Gardens in Janesville, Wisconsin, for 21 years.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois.
  • Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”.

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

According to recent reports, the garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

In a recent development, the garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

It has been revealed that jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

In a recent development, last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

According to recent reports, the Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and initiative your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

It has been revealed that creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a new window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

In a recent development, on the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

#158938. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1060 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
  • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
  • In a recent development, design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

In a recent development, design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

Sources indicate that in a newly introduced garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

Privacy was one of the massive considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

In a recent development, looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

According to recent reports, what a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

It has been revealed that growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

In a recent development, I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from major cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build fresh nests.

Sources indicate that the ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.
